data.title: Trump says he offered White House press secretary job to Dana White
data.description:
President Trump said he offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

In a Truth Social post on Saturday, Trump said that he requested White bring “assistants” with him and named several UFC fighters.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote. “I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris.”

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

Rapid Response 47 also posted a screenshot of Trump’s Truth Social post on the social platform X.

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request to confirm the offer. It is unclear whether White has accepted the position.

data.title: Meet Stephen Miller, Trump's new chief of staff: 5 things to know
data.description:
President Trump announced Friday that longtime White House aide Stephen Miller would be his next chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles — who has served in the role since Trump returned to office.

Miller is an immigration hardliner and Trump loyalist who has been with the president since he launched his first campaign. The promotion was highly controversial among Democrats and even some Republicans, who see Miller as partly responsible for the GOP’s midterm losses, when the part lost control of the House and Senate and Democrats won large majorities.

Here are five things to know about Stephen Miller.

Former Sessions staffer

Miller started his career in Washington working as a press secretary for Rep. Michele Bachmann (R-Minn) in 2007 and later for Rep. John Shadegg (R-Ariz.). In 2009, he served as Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions’s press secretary before moving up the ranks — becoming his communications chief.

Miller pushed Sessions to become more outspoken and combative, especially on the issue of immigration. He helped Sessions kill a bipartisan immigration reform bill in 2013 by writing a handbook to help lawmakers defeat it.

Behind the scenes, Miller carved out an inside-the-Beltway reputation as a hard-charging press aide, frequently battling with reporters and others in Washington.

When Trump announced his run for the presidency in 2015, Sessions became the first senator to endorse him. The Alabama senator went onto to serve as the president’s attorney general during his first stint in the White House.

But Sessions eventually fell out with Trump after recusing himself from investigations into Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and election win.

Miller, in contrast, became a part of Trump’s inner circle and was a confidant to the president for the rest of his first term, his years out of office and during his second term.

Hardline immigration enforcer

Miller is considered the architect behind much of Trump’s immigration policies — most recently his administration’s mass deportation efforts.

As deputy chief of staff for policy, Miller pushed the administration to suspend habeas corpus rights, which allow people in custody to challenge their detention, and triple its daily immigration arrest goals to 3,000.

One of the administration’s most high-profile immigration blitzes in Trump’s second term was “Operation Metro Surge” in Minneapolis, during which federal agents fatally shot two American citizens. Miller at the time called both victims “domestic terrorists.” 

In the first Trump administration, Miller was also a primary advocate of the administration’s family separation policy.

Consummate Washington insider

Before his promotion to chief of staff, Miller was already in the president’s ear as a key policy adviser. He will now be one of the top voices in the Trump White House and among other influential people in Washington.

Miller is one of the only aides from Trump’s first term to be serving in a high role in his second term. He has a deep understanding of how Washington runs, and is known to dig deep into policy matters. His background as a Senate aide gives him a strong understanding of how Congress works, and on how executive authority can be used to assert presidential power.

During debates over legislation affecting immigration, Miller was seen as having a big influence on the stance Republicans took. He is known as a detail-oriented aide who reads briefs, asks questions and demands results.

As chief of staff, Miller will be able to have his fingers on everything the White House touches. Wiles, the outgoing chief, was seen by some as a brake on Miller. With her gone, that brake would be lost just as Miller takes what has histocially been seen as the second most powerful role at the White House, behind only the president himself.

The chief of staff works closely with the president on day-to-day operations and manages the White House staff. It can be a gatekeeper role for how sees the president and can be a position involved in all policy decisions, depending on the individual chief of staff.

It is a role that does not require Senate confirmation.

Miller’s wife, Katie Miller — a GOP political adviser and podcaster — has also established herself during Trump’s time in office and is well-connected in Republican circles. During the first term, she served as communications director and press secretary to then Vice President Pence.

When Trump returned to office, Katie Miller became an adviser to the controversial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), an Elon Musk-led initiative to slash government spending and reduce the size of the workforce.

Katie Miller now hosts a podcast, “The Katie Miller Podcast,” directed at conservative women.

Early Trump loyalist

Many in the president’s orbit have come and gone over the past decade — including Wiles, who had a brief falling out with Trump before returning to run his campaign in 2024.

But Miller has remained loyal the entire time, from the 2016 campaign to both his terms in the White House.

When Trump lost reelection in 2020, Miller co-founded America First Legal, a conservative nonprofit advocating for dismantling diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, enforcing immigration laws and protecting election integrity.

Miller rejoined Trump’s 2024 campaign and returned to the White House right away as deputy chief of staff for policy and an adviser on homeland security.

Divisive GOP figure

While most of the criticism around Miller’s promotion came from Democrats, some Republicans questioned whether Trump was making the right choice in light of sweeping midterm losses.

No critic of Miller in the GOP is louder than Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who told the president to “rethink” his decision to promote the deputy chief. The North Carolina Republican has repeatedly criticized Miller’s immigration stance and accused him of giving the president bad advice.

“It is a colossal mistake, and the last thing we need 72 hours after the a– whooping we got on Tuesday,” Tillis told CNN Friday.

Even some former Trump administration officials questioned the move.

Sarah Matthews, a former deputy White House press secretary, called the notion of replacing Wiles with Miller “terrifying.”

Another former Trump administration official told The Hill Miller’s promotion is “exactly the opposite” direction from what voters demanded.

“It’s exactly the opposite direction voters are begging Republicans to go. Susie was the best thing that happened to President Trump,” the official said.

A former Trump chief of staff said choosing Miller is not likely to help the president forge a working relationship with the new Democratic majority.

data.title: President Trump: Forget the midterms and finish the job in Iran
data.description:
Vice President JD Vance and Iran would like Americans to blame the war and Israel for the Republicans’ midterm electoral drubbing. President Trump, however, disagrees. He should rise above this noise and refocus on the U.S. national interest by fulfilling his repeated vow to “finish the job” with Iran.

In announcing Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, Trump articulated five key American goals: “destroy their missiles,” “annihilate their Navy,” “ensure the regime’s terrorist proxies can no longer destabilize the region or the world,” “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon” and “unleash [Iran’s] prosperous and glorious future.”

These original objectives have been pared back over time. The first to fall away, almost immediately, was Trump’s directive to the Iranian people to “take over your government.” By April, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine no longer mentioned ending Iran’s support for terrorism.

Trump walked back the goal of destroying Iran’s projectile threat, suggesting in June that “missiles aren’t the problem.” And, most recently, Vance put an end to demanding the end of Iran’s nuclear program, asking only for a “meaningful” reduction in enrichment. 

All that remains of the original U.S. war aims is annihilating Iran’s navy, which is both already accomplished and largely irrelevant to Iran’s threat.  

Operation Epic Fury has notched significant accomplishments. Trump overstates the case when he claims that Iran has “been systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially,” but seriously damaged would be correct. Iran’s nuclear program and defense industrial base still lie under rubble. Its economic lifeblood, oil exports, has been largely choked off. A whole tier of military and civilian leaders was eliminated.  

But that’s not enough.  

Iran rebuilt its conventional military capabilities far quicker than expected after last year’s 12-Day War and could do so again. While most of Iran’s 60 percent enriched uranium was entombed by U.S. B-2 bombers, Iran still could access it.  The U.S. and Israel reportedly had a plan to get it out, using ground forces, but Trump opted against it. Pickaxe Mountain, dangerous because of how deeply buried it is, was not even targeted either in last year’s war or this year’s.  

Rather than be forced back into conflict by a rearmed Iran, the U.S. and Israel can and should, as Trump has said, finish the job by returning to and fulfilling his original five objectives. That means the U.S. and Israel need to soon launch a new, short but intense campaign of strikes against Iran’s remaining missile and drone facilities, coastal radars, batteries, small boat launches and air defenses.  

This operation should also set the conditions for rendering inoperable Iran’s nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, and eliminating its 60 percent enriched uranium, with a ground operation as necessary. U.S. strikes should also target a portion of Iran’s domestic energy infrastructure, further weakening the regime’s hold on power, and clearly signal that Iranian retaliation will prompt further such strikes.

Such a campaign will entail risks. U.S. forces and our Israeli and Arab allies’ homelands will come under Iranian fire. Fuel prices will likely spike, at least temporarily. But the alternative, leaving the Iranian threat in place, is riskier and costlier still.

But Iran’s missiles, drones, proxies, navy and nukes are not the primary threats. Even if they were fully destroyed, Iran would attempt to rebuild them or find new means of aggression. The threat is the Iranian regime and its determination to destroy America, Israel and the West at any cost. Thus, even a new round of strikes will not finish the job. The U.S. will have to remain vigilant, monitoring Iran and potentially returning for additional strikes to stop it from reconstituting.  

The war will only end by returning to the first objective Trump dropped from his list: the collapse of the fanatical, barbaric Tehran regime. No deal should be made with Iran; it would only sustain the regime. The U.S. military’s blockade is vital to further weakening it and accelerating its demise.  

But more is needed: encouraging defections, fomenting distrust and friction among regime factions and strengthening opposition within Iran, providing everything from public statements of support to covert arms shipments to enable the Iranian people to overcome the regime’s violent forces and dispatch the Islamic Republic to the dustbin of history.  

The midterms changed the political landscape in Washington but not the geopolitical chessboard in the Middle East. The Iranian threat remains; removing it is still the only way to end the war.  

Michael Makovsky, Ph.D., a former Department of Defense official, is president and CEO of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America. Blaise Misztal is vice president for Policy at JINSA.

data.title: Trump's glide path to judicial confirmations comes to an end
data.description:
Democrats’ Senate victory means President Trump for the first time will lose a glide path to nominate judges and Supreme Court justices.  

Pressure had grown on conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito to retire, but they show no sign of imminently stepping down. 

And Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) is already signaling the party, burned by past confirmation fights, could be a roadblock if a Supreme Court vacancy ever arises in the new Congress. 

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview. 

It’s a major shift in dynamics after Trump’s remaking of the federal courts became one of his most lasting first-term legacies. 

He nominated dozens of lower court judges and three justices to the Supreme Court — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — to cement its 6-3 conservative majority. 

That legacy carried over to the lower courts, too. By this point in his first term, the Senate had confirmed 83 of Trump’s judicial nominees, according to Federal Judicial Center data. 

With Democrats set to take over the Senate majority and the chamber’s advice and consent power on the president’s nominees in a matter of weeks, a continued climb is increasingly in jeopardy. And the confirmation pace was already slower this term, with 56 confirmed so far, according to the data. 

It’s left some Republicans calling for a swift push on the remaining lower court openings before the new Congress begins in January.

“Every single federal judicial vacancy needs to be filled in the lame duck session,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) wrote on social media Friday. “The Senate should pull all-nighters for as long as it takes. Democrats wont confirm a single Trump judge once they take over.” 

Twenty-eight district court vacancies are waiting to be filled, with nominees pending for 11 of them, according to the federal judiciary’s administrative office.  

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) called on the Senate to confirm U.S. district court nominee Robert Long, saying he’s one of the “finest jurists” and lamenting that his nomination has been pending for months. 

Mike Davis, a close legal ally of the president, ramped up pressure on Arkansas’s Republican senators — Tom Cotton and John Boozman — to confirm Lee Rudofsky to an appeals court seat. Rudofsky serves in a trial judgeship in Arkansas, and Davis accused the senators of having “wanted someone else.” 

“They need to change their minds–and fast–or Republicans will lose this key appellate court seat,” Davis wrote on social platform X. 

Spokespeople for Cotton and Boozman did not return a request for comment. 

The president appears set to continue announcing new names as the lame-duck session begins. James Sullivan, who is projected to lose his seat on the Texas Supreme Court in this week’s elections, is set to be nominated to a federal judgeship, according to a questionnaire submitted to the Senate this week first reported by Reuters.

The midterms have also shifted the political dynamics for Supreme Court vacancies. 

In Trump’s first term, Democrats accused Republicans of stealing Supreme Court seats for Gorsuch and Barrett. They voted against Kavanaugh over sexual assault accusations that he denies. But Democrats never had the votes to block the nominations after Republicans eliminated the filibuster for Supreme Court nominees.
 
Now, Democrats are expressing glee with the party projected to win at least 54 Senate seats, including in red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. Depending on how the races in Alaska and Mississippi shake out, the party could ultimately win as many as 56 seats heading into the new Congress.

Some outside pressure had grown on Thomas, 78, and Alito, 76, the court’s two oldest conservative justices, to step down ahead of the election to ensure Trump could send a replacement while the Senate remained under Republicans’ control.  

Many of those voices pointed to the late liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who remained on the court despite liberal pressure until her 2020 death, enabling Trump to replace her just days before the presidential election.

As pressure grew on Alito and Thomas, others on the right condemned the talk. Leonard Leo, the judicial activist who played a central role in the Supreme Court’s conservative shift, publicly called the retirement speculation “crass.” Even Trump put the talk to the side. 

“I hope they stay, ’cause I think they’re fantastic, OK?” Trump said last year.  

Ultimately, Alito told CBS News in an interview that aired last month that he “thought about” stepping down but decided against it. 

“It’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term. But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place,” he said. 

Following Democrats’ win, Alito has again told people he does not plan to immediately step down, according to reports from The New York Times and Bloomberg. Alito did not return The Hill’s request for comment about his plans. 

Thomas, meanwhile, recently became the second-longest-serving justice in American history. Many court watchers expect he’ll set the record — a feat he’ll reach in May 2028.  

Although they are the court’s oldest members at 78 and 76, respectively, Thomas and Alito are still younger than recent justices who’ve retired. 

Justice Stephen Breyer served until he was nearly 84. Justice Anthony Kennedy had just turned 82 on his last day. Before him, Justice John Paul Stevens served until age 90.  

The most recent justice to retire younger than the duo’s ages was Justice David Souter, who stepped down in 2009 at the age of 69 to return to a quieter life in New Hampshire.

data.title: Are hackers targeting America's food supply?
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A series of cyberattacks on grocery stores out of Europe have raised concerns about cyber threats stateside as the U.S. government warns businesses of potential attacks targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

What have US officials said?

Brett Leatherman, head of the FBI Cyber Division, spoke in an advisory warning Thursday, urging organizations to take mitigation steps against potential malicious cyber actors immediately.

“These systems protect food and medicine across health care, food and agriculture, and other critical sectors here in the United States as well. Attackers are getting in through controllers that are unpatched, reachable from the internet, or still using the default passwords listed in the manufacturer’s manual,” said Leatherman.

In a joint warning from the FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services (HHS) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), experts urged organizations to eliminate public internet exposure, isolate operational technology and enforce credential security to mitigate potential attacks.

A grave warning from ex-FBI

Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker spoke with Fox News to warn Americans further, interpreting the cyberattacks as a form of “asymmetrical warfare,” where opponents use unconventional tactics to expose the vulnerabilities of a stronger opponent.

“This asymmetrical warfare has a very strong psychological impact, but we’re Americans. We will not falter ever,” she said.

Parker also urged citizens to keep food, water, medication and other supplies on hand in case of a wider cyberattack

What is the state of cybersecurity in the US?

Experts dubbed the most recent month “Black October” in reference to the intense wave of software vulnerabilities and high-profile cyber incidents driven by AI. A senior director of product management at Figma wrote in an Oct. 22 X post following a surge in PHP attacks,

“In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year.”

In late August, at least six American military bases suffered freezer malfunctions, and U.S. cyber investigators partnered with French law enforcement to research the potential hacks.

What happened in Europe?

In Europe, over 350 supermarkets and several French blood banks reported temperature rises in cold equipment up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, forcing suppliers to throw out shelves of spoiled food, losses which may cost tens of millions of euros. While the French Blood Establishment said its surveillance systems were triggered and taken offline, no blood products were lost during the attack, with the samples promptly transported to other facilities.

The hacks came in two waves, one that hit in the middle of October and another impacting grocery stores just days ago.

A top cybersecurity official from Romania characterized the threat as “semi-amateurish,” speaking to the AFP news agency. He added, “We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”

data.title: Plane etiquette is getting worse, survey finds. These are the biggest offenses
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Long gone are the days when air travel was seen as a luxurious experience – at least for those of us stuck toward the back of the plane. Now, it’s more likely to be something you dread. 

Many people think the flying experience has gotten worse, according to a survey of 2,500 people by YouGov and The Points Guy, but it’s not just because of smaller seats and abundant delays. Fellow passengers are often to blame for the misery. 

When asked to rank the most annoying behaviors on board a flight, the No. 1 worst offender was noise. Whether it’s talking loudly, blasting music or watching videos without headphones, 27% of survey respondents said general noisiness was the most irritating airplane behavior they frequently encounter.

The second most annoying behavior is the infamous seat recline, specifically people who lay all the way back unnecessarily or without warning. 

The debate over whether or not it’s polite to recline on a flight has heated up since airlines have moved to tighter seating arrangements with less legroom. If you’d like to lean back without ticking off the passenger behind you, survey respondents said it’s best to ask first. 

“Mind the speed in which you recline your seat,” former flight attendant and etiquette expert Elaine Swann told Nexstar. “Take a moment to just turn and glance backward [at the person in the seat behind you], like checking your rearview mirror. … You might be able to see a beverage or a laptop on the tray, and if so, that should guide you.” 

Finally, one of the most annoying passenger behaviors actually comes after the flight is over: rushing to deplane. 

A majority of respondents believed the best way to offboard is row by row, front to back. But anyone who has flown recently knows people will often jump up and start inching their way forward before it’s “their turn.” Only 10% of survey respondents thought it was OK to move ahead if there’s an opening, but 65% said it’s best to wait until your row is next in line.

data.title: Higher ed affordability is about more than tuition
data.description:
Higher education media is filled with articles describing a decline or “collapse of confidence” in higher education. But it is important to clarify what we are actually seeing. 

A recent Gallup-Lumina Foundation study of 14,000 adults between the ages of 18 and 59 found that Americans still believe higher education is important, particularly for career advancement, and they feel that college degrees still matter as much as they did 20 years ago. Interest in enrolling also remains high, with 58 percent stating that they have considered pursuing a degree or credential within the last two years.

At the same time, confidence has declined in another sense. While people believe that higher education matters and would make a difference in their careers, a growing number of them do not believe they can afford it. Moreover, despite the benefits of having a degree, people are unsure if the cumulative costs of pursuing one justifies those benefits. 

This, and other factors, contributes to enrollment pressures for colleges and universities. A natural reaction for institutions would be to address tuition affordability. But there’s a risk of overly focusing on tuition when, in reality, the issue of affordability is a multi-faceted one — especially for adult learners.

The tuition bill captures only one part of what students must pay when they enroll in a degree program. For adult learners in particular, other costs include lost wages from reduced work hours, managing childcare or elder care, potential relocation or housing expenses, transportation, opportunities lost at work due to conflicts with coursework and rigid course schedules that can force students to stay enrolled longer than a program’s curriculum technically requires. 

Due to these hidden costs, a program can look affordable on paper but still be financially and pragmatically out of reach for many students.   

Flexibility is often treated as a matter of scheduling and access, but it impacts affordability as well. Program structure can impact wages, relocation, housing, commuting, childcare or elder care and invisible costs such as meals and parking. 

Transportation is a good example. A 2023 report from the Trellis Company found that transportation accounted for almost 20 percent of the cost of attending college for commuters, and the College Board estimated an average annual transportation budget of $2,070 for students commuting to public two-year colleges.

Online options can eliminate much of that expense but are just one form of flexibility.  Studies published in 2023 and 2026 found that asynchronous options help adult learners manage jobs and childcare, alleviate time-related stress and reduce dropout intentions resulting from time constraints.  

Part-time options can also allow adult learners to continue working full-time. Letting students start programs at multiple points throughout the year, instead of just in the spring and fall, can reduce long waiting periods before starting a program. It is also not uncommon for students to have to interrupt their education due to life circumstances. Letting them pause their courses and return when they’re able can prevent temporary disruptions from becoming permanent withdrawals.  

Another reason why higher education can feel so unaffordable for many is the traditional all-or-nothing model which provides little value unless the degree program is fully completed. From the perspective of adult learners, this is a considerable risk in terms of the time and money invested. Stackable credentials and certificates at key milestones can reduce that risk, and research has linked these pathways to higher rates of reenrollment and additional credential attainment.  

The answer is not unlimited course structures, scheduling and credential pathways. Just as limited options create barriers, too many options without enough structure can create confusion, extend completion time and increase costs.

Adding stackable credentials into a program must be done in ways that allow those credits to satisfy requirements for the degree a student eventually wants to earn. If, for example, only six of the credits in a 12-credit certificate apply to a student’s degree program, the student ends up having to take more courses than if they had simply pursued the degree directly from the outset. 

Clear, structured and predictable pathways are needed. And institutions should communicate key information for every credential and degree: required courses, course sequencing, when courses will be offered, expected time to completion, total likely cost and what options may be available in the event students need to pause their study.  

Institutions cannot eliminate every financial pressure that students face. However, they can reduce the unnecessary financial risks, uncertainties and stress caused by overly limited options, rigid schedules, all-or-nothing degree structures or confusing credential pathways. The institutions that respond most effectively to the affordability crisis in higher education will be the ones that treat affordability as not just a question of tuition and fees, but of program design as well. 

By combining meaningful flexibility with clear, structured pathways toward credentials and degrees, institutions can give students a more realistic opportunity to pursue the higher education that they continue to believe can enhance their lives. 

Evan Kropp, Ph.D. is the executive director of Distance Education at the University of Florida College of Journalism and Communications.

data.title: Miller calls chief of staff promotion 'honor of my life' at Mar-a-Lago event
data.description:
Longtime White House aide Stephen Miller pledged his “absolute loyalty” to President Trump in short remarks Friday evening shortly after being promoted to chief of staff — replacing Susie Wiles

“We need to stand with the man who has stood with us with every fiber of his being,” Miller said in a video Trump posted to Truth Social. “I pledge you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

Giving quick remarks at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Fla., Miller called the promotion “the honor of my life.”

Trump announced Friday morning that Wiles, who had served as chief of staff since he returned to office, had stepped down and Miller would replace her.

The choice quickly sparked backlash from Democrats and some Republicans, who said the president learned the wrong lesson from sweeping midterm losses.

“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote in a post on the social platform X. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice.”

Miller was the architect behind much of the president’s hardline immigration policies, including mass deportation efforts in his second term. Democrats have slammed Miller for his rhetoric in the past, namely after he called the two American citizens killed during federal immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis “domestic terrorists.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Friday the president should “rethink” his decision to elevate Miller, calling it a “colossal mistake” after the party’s midterm losses.

“This past Tuesday, Republicans lost because we lost the narrative on the border, a success that the president should have been heralding,” Tillis said. “Now we’re talking about putting one of the most partisan, polarizing figures, and not only polarizing in terms of Republicans and Democrats, but even among Republicans.”

Trump’s cabinet secretaries broadly praised the switch, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who shared a photo of himself and Miller with the caption, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”

Millers’s chief of staff appointment brings Hegseth even closer to the White House as the Pentagon chief faces growing backlash for his leadership and handling of the Iran war. House Oversight Committee chair James Comer (R-Ky.) admitted, “There’s a lot of questions about Hegseth” as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) renews his push to impeach the defense secretary.

But Miller seemed to sing the praises of the second Trump administration’s defense agenda Friday night, saying, “If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America. He saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our boarder from annihilation. And he saved our country from threats from home and abroad.”

data.title: A 'reverse-Ginsberg' scenario could flip the Supreme Court without packing
data.description:
In Henry VI, Shakespeare wrote, “Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends.” Many today would like to chisel those words above the doors to the Supreme Court. Time and time again, justices waited too long for their own legacies.

For many conservatives, the decisive loss of both houses of Congress has created a true nightmare scenario in which two conservatives (Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito) could hand Democrats the opportunity to take control of the Supreme Court without having to carry out their court-packing schemes. Control of the court could now be lost by sheer attrition.

Timing has always been a looming question for justices who want to see their seats filled by like-minded jurists. However, it is difficult to walk away from being one of nine.

Some served beyond their own capabilities in clinging to the court, becoming befuddled and isolated with age. That was the case with iconic justices such as William Douglas and Thurgood Marshall.

Others stayed too long to guarantee the preservation of their own legacies. The most recent example is Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Some of us wrote for years that Ginsburg was risking her legacy by not retiring while Barack Obama was president. After President Trump replaced her with Justice Amy Coney Barrett, many liberals (who were consciously silent before her death) lamented her decision.

Now, conservatives worry they may face a double tap. For two years, there has been speculation that Thomas (78) and Alito (76) might retire to allow a Republican president and Republican Senate to select their successors. Both declined to do so.

If they were hoping for a two-year cushion, that window just closed with a resounding bang. Even if they were to resign in the next two years, it is unlikely that Trump could replace either with a conservative nominee.

With at least 54 Senate seats (and perhaps as many as 56), the Democrats do not fear defections from independent-minded senators like Sen. John Fetterman (D., N.J.). They will also cite the denial of a vote for Merrick Garland during the Obama administration as a justification for denying a vote to Trump nominees.

Even before the election, liberals had raised money to campaign against even prospective nominees for Trump.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris called for Democratic donors to oppose “additional justices” that might be nominated by Trump “before they happen.” She praised the fundraising by Josh Orton, president of the dark-money group “Demand Justice.” It was a notable endorsement, since Demand Justice was infamous for its campaign to get Justice Stephen Breyer to resign, including mobile billboards reading “Breyer, retire. Don’t risk your legacy.” Demand Justice has also pushed a radical agenda, including court-packing.

Of course, Breyer did resign, allowing Biden to replace him with Ketanji Brown Jackson, arguably the farthest-left justice to ever sit on the court.

As soon as the Democrats took control, the Senate Minority Leader (and possible incoming Majority Leader) Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) declared that they would bar “any crappy nominees,” which was taken to mean any Trump nominee.

In fairness to Thomas and Alito, neither is diminished by age. Both have appeared in public and shown they are fully capable and effective. In the cases of Douglass and Marshall, they were eventually pressured to resign after they appeared on television and were clearly enfeebled.

The last two years have seen some of the most important opinions from Thomas and Alito in their careers on the court. Now, however, they could be looking at not two more years but six more years to wait for a Republican president if the midterms foreshadow the 2028 election.

If so, by the time a Republican could succeed such a Democrat, Thomas would be roughly 84 and Alito 82. And the Senate may not even then be ready to confirm like-minded successors.

The risk is tremendous. If their vacancies cause a reverse Ginsburg, the court would shift from a 6-3 majority favoring conservatives to a 5-4 majority favoring liberals.

Worse yet, in the calls to pack the court with a liberal majority, politicians and pundits often point to Biden-appointee Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as the model. Jackson has been widely criticized for a radical jurisprudence that discards longstanding norms and doctrines, including by her two liberal colleagues.

Such a court would make court packing entirely unnecessary. The signature opinions of Thomas and Alito would likely fall in quick succession, from Thomas’s gun rights decision in Bruen to Alito’s abortion ruling in Dobbs.

Nevertheless, it is much to ask for two jurists to resign when they are both mentally and physically capable, particularly after rendering some of their most influential opinions in the last two years.

Some believe that justices should not engage in strategic resignations to shape the ideology of the Court. These justices, they reason, have a right to serve out their lifetime appointments as long as they can do the job. They can have a clear conscience serving as long as they are able, and leave their replacements to the will of the American people.

In any case, with less than six weeks left with a Republican Senate, the time has effectively run out for the retirement option in holding these seats for conservatives. 

The irony is that these two justices can take considerable credit in the building of the conservative jurisprudence that has emerged in recent years on the court. They have shown great patience in building the authority to overturn longstanding cases, from Roe v. Wade to Humphrey’s Executor. That legacy may now rest with their own longevity in the years to come.

Jonathan Turley is the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: US military targets Iranian defense system in latest round of limited strikes
data.description:
The U.S. launched new defensive strikes against Iran targeting the country’s air defense systems, President Trump said on Friday, describing the strikes as “minor.”

The U.S. military previously struck Iran on Monday, just a day before the midterms, targeting Iran’s Qeshm Island, home to an Iranian naval base and in the critical Strait of Hormuz. Trump had previously said he would not strike Iran until after the midterms.

Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island on Friday, according to the Associated Press, and posted on social media that the Iranian army had shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm.

“The Islamic Republic of Iran Army announced that an MQ-9 drone belonging to what it called the aggressive American enemy was hit and brought down over Qeshm,” state media said on the social platform X.

The strikes ahead of the midterms were not publicly acknowledged by the Pentagon, which had not disclosed any attacks on Iranian targets since early September.

Friday’s strikes mark the first since the midterm elections, in which the war was a major issue for voters.

The final Reuters/Ipsos survey ahead of the midterms found that just 33 percent of Americans approved of the Iran war, while 62 percent disapproved.

After the Republicans’ election wipeout — in which the GOP lost at least eight Senate seats and dozens of House seats — many in the party blamed the Iran war for losses, including Vice President Vance.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote in a long social media post after the election.

“Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he added.

Trump seemed to agree with Vance and admitted in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that the war was part of the reason for the party’s fate.

Even Iran chimed in after the election, with its speaker of parliament writing on X, “Americans said NO TO WAR.”

The war, now in its ninth month, was projected by the president and his administration to last only a few weeks when it began in February. But negotiations have fallen apart between the two sides more than once, and at the heart of them is the critical Strait of Hormuz. Iranian attacks in the strait throughout the war sent gas and diesel prices surging worldwide.

The U.S. recorded its highest-ever Election Day average gas price Tuesday as voters went to the polls.
